Products have higher binding energy per nucleon → less total mass → Δmc² released.
Neutrons from one fission trigger more fissions; steady if on average one neutron per fission does so.
Minimum mass for a self-sustaining chain reaction — fewer neutrons escape.
Slows neutrons to thermal speeds (water, graphite).
Absorb neutrons (boron, cadmium) to control the fission rate.
Exchanger: transfers energy to make steam. Shielding: absorbs neutrons and γ to protect people.
Cooling ponds → reprocessing → vitrify and store deep underground.

front: Are fast neutrons best at causing fission of U-235?
back: No — slow (thermal, ~0.025 eV) neutrons are far more likely to be absorbed by U-235. Fission produces fast neutrons, hence the moderator.

front: Energy released in a fission reaction from binding energies?
back: $E = (\text{total BE of products}) - (\text{total BE of reactants}) = \Delta m\,c^2$.

front: About 200 MeV is released per U-235 fission. In joules?
back: $200\times10^6 \times 1.60\times10^{-19} \approx 3.2\times10^{-11}$ J — mostly as kinetic energy of the fragments.
Fission triggered when a nucleus (e.g. U-235) absorbs a neutron, forming an unstable nucleus (U-236) that splits.

front: Subcritical, critical and supercritical chain reactions?
back: On average fewer than one / exactly one / more than one neutron per fission causes a further fission: dying out / steady (reactor) / growing rapidly.

front: Why are moderators made of light nuclei such as hydrogen (water) or carbon (graphite)?
back: In an elastic collision a neutron loses the most energy to a nucleus of similar mass, so fewer collisions are needed to slow it to thermal speeds.
The moderator **slows** neutrons (increasing the fission probability). Control rods **absorb** neutrons (reducing the fission rate).
Increasing the proportion of fissile U-235 from about 0.7 % in natural uranium to about 3–5 % for reactor fuel.

front: Energy transfers in a nuclear power station?
back: Nuclear → kinetic energy of fragments → thermal energy of coolant → steam (heat exchanger) → kinetic energy of turbine → electrical energy (generator).

front: Does a reactor produce electricity directly?
back: No. It produces thermal energy; turbines and generators convert that to electricity, as in a fossil-fuel station.

front: Why is spent fuel hazardous for so long?
back: It contains fission products and transuranic elements (e.g. plutonium) that are highly radioactive and some of which have half-lives of thousands of years.

front: Main advantages and disadvantages of fission power?
back: For: no CO₂ in operation, very high energy density, reliable baseload. Against: long-lived radioactive waste, risk of accidents, cost, weapons proliferation.
